extracted.intended_audience: readers of an annotated edition of The Spectator; literary-historical readers and students
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated excerpt from early-18th-century Spectator essays with editorial notes and commentary. Contains prose essays, critical observations on taste, theatre, medicine, and political pamphleteering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of panegyric
rubrics_metrics.description: "The perfection of which was asserted to consist in a certain artful way of conveying the applause in an indirect manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: praising by surprise (e.g., proposing Tiberius should be declared a god) wins instant favour; a compliment that takes a man by surprise is effective because it reverses expectations and makes the flatterer welcome. Several illustrative anecdotes are given to show the effectiveness of indirect or unexpected praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising flattery as a rhetorical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden, unexpected praise disarms hostility and gains immediate access to the favoured person's goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by anecdotes: the senator's proposal about Tiberius; an instance where a benefactor denies having influenced an appointment (making the recipient more grateful). Guidance: use surprise and indirectness to secure favour; avoid obvious or clumsy flattery which may provoke suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility versus sublimity in pamphlet/political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A pamphlet described as having "language [that] is extremely sublime, and not at all to be understood by the vulgar" may thereby limit its readership and sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical observation: overly elevated, abstruse style (even when praising) can be an anti-pattern because it alienates common readers and reduces impact. The passage counsels awareness of audience comprehension when choosing rhetorical register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage morality and decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was against all morality, as well as rules of the stage, that Punch should be in jest in the Deluge, or indeed that he should appear at all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for theatrical representation: avoid introducing buffoonery or jest into sacred or morally serious scenes; mixing incongruous comic elements (e.g., Punch) with solemn subject-matter breaches both morality and established stage rules. Example: contemporary critic hissing at Punch-in-Deluge episode as improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'wit' (Virgilian standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit, by Virgil's representation, is allied to virtue: 'the wisest man was the greatest wit; and none was thought worthy of that character, unless he answered this excellent description of the poet' — one who places happiness in contempt of low fears and mean gratifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical standard for judging a man of letters: intellectual brilliance (wit) is ideally coupled with moral greatness — contempt of petty fears and base pleasures. Use this moralized conception of wit when evaluating literary character and public reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure requires severity (res est severa voluptas)
rubrics_metrics.description: "res est severa voluptas" — there is a certain severity in pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic/social guideline: true pleasure involves a degree of moderation and reason; unchecked appetite or absence of decency makes human pleasures miserable. Applied as a norm for manners and taste: decency and reason should attend even convivial pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward quacks and evaluating medical credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Take heed whom you trust in physick, for it's become a common cheat to profess it. He gives his opinion to all that writes or comes for nothing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: be wary of practitioners who offer indiscriminate or gratuitous medical opinions; check credentials and reputation (references to sworn physicians in ordinary to the king are used as markers). The text treats quackery as common and cautions against trusting self-professed healers.
